explain.say: Close your eyes and touch your nose. You can do it because of proprioception, the sense of where your body parts are and how they are moving. Some people call it a sixth sense.

faq.a: Proprioception is your sense of where your body parts are and how they are moving, without looking. It comes from sensors in muscles, tendons and joints.
Muscle spindles are tiny stretch sensors wrapped in nerve endings, found inside muscles. They report how long a muscle is and how quickly it is stretching, which tells the brain where the limb is.
Tendon sensors, called Golgi tendon organs, sit where muscles join tendons. They measure how hard a muscle is pulling, helping you judge force, like lifting an egg gently or a bag firmly.

faq.q: How does the brain know where my arms are?
faq.a: The brain combines signals from muscle spindles, tendon sensors, joints and skin into a constantly updated map of the body. Vision and the balance organs add extra checks.
asks: How do we know where our arms are without looking?
What is the body map in the brain?

faq.q: How can I touch my nose with my eyes closed?
faq.a: Your proprioception tells your brain exactly where your hand and head are, so it can guide your finger to your nose without seeing it. This simple test is used to check that the system is working.
asks: Why can I find my nose in the dark?
Touch your nose eyes closed test

facts: Proprioception comes mainly from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs and joint receptors.
The finger-to-nose test is a classic way of checking body-position sense and coordination.

quiz.say: Which sensors report how stretched a muscle is?
quiz.why: Muscle spindles are stretch sensors inside muscles that report length and speed of stretch.

wrong.1: Taste buds sense chemicals in food.
wrong.2: Cone cells in the eye sense light and colour.
